home.lead: Enter an old value and a new value to see the percentage increase straight away, with the formula and every step shown. You can also work out a decrease, a change, a difference, or find the original number before a percentage was added.
what: Percentage increase tells you how much a number has grown, compared with where it started. It is shown as a percentage of the starting (old) value, so a rise from 50 to 75 is a 50% increase: the number grew by half of its original size.

Because the starting value is the reference point, the same gap can give different percentages depending on direction. Going from 50 to 75 is a 50% increase, but going back from 75 to 50 is only a 33.33% decrease.
home.formulaMain: Percentage increase = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100
formulaNotes: Subtract the old value from the new value to get the increase.
Divide that increase by the old value.
Multiply by 100 to turn the decimal into a percentage.
A negative answer means the value went down, so it is a decrease.

examples.title: A price goes up
examples.body: A pair of shoes costs $80 and the price rises to $100. The increase is $100 − $80 = $20. Then $20 ÷ $80 = 0.25, and 0.25 × 100 = 25%. The price went up by 25%.

examples.title: A pay rise
examples.body: Your salary goes from $40,000 to $44,000. The increase is $4,000. Then $4,000 ÷ $40,000 = 0.1, so the pay rise is 10%.

examples.title: Website visitors
examples.body: A blog had 1,200 visitors last month and 1,830 this month. The increase is 630. Then 630 ÷ 1,200 = 0.525, so traffic grew by 52.5%.

examples.title: A decrease
examples.body: A phone drops in price from $250 to $200. The change is $200 − $250 = −$50. Then −$50 ÷ $250 = −0.2, which is −20%. The price fell by 20%.

examples.title: Increase a number by a percentage
examples.body: To add 15% to 60, first find 15% of 60: 60 × 0.15 = 9. Then add it: 60 + 9 = 69. You can also do it in one step: 60 × 1.15 = 69.

faq.q: How do I calculate percentage increase?
faq.a: Subtract the old value from the new value, divide the result by the old value, then multiply by 100. For example, from 20 to 25: (25 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 25%.

faq.q: Can a percentage increase be more than 100%?
faq.a: Yes. If a value more than doubles, the increase is above 100%. Going from 10 to 35 is an increase of 250%.

faq.q: What if the old value is zero?
faq.a: The percentage increase is undefined, because the formula divides by the old value and you cannot divide by zero. This calculator shows a message instead of a result.

faq.q: Is a percentage increase the same as percentage points?
faq.a: No. If a rate moves from 4% to 6%, it rises by 2 percentage points, but the percentage increase is (6 − 4) ÷ 4 × 100 = 50%.

faq.q: Why is the decrease smaller than the increase going back?
faq.a: Each percentage is measured against a different starting value. A rise from 50 to 75 is +50%, while the drop from 75 back to 50 is −33.33%.

faq.q: How do I find the original value before a percentage increase?
faq.a: Divide the final value by 1 plus the percentage as a decimal. If a price is 120 after a 20% rise, the original was 120 ÷ 1.2 = 100. Choose the reverse percentage option above to do this.
